doc.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023

title: Apostolic church teaching on money and her mother's Gospel group
summary: The Apostolic Singers, her grandfather's group and the film about it; the faith frowns on earning money from music, a lifelong conflict; her aunt was her first piano model.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: So your mother was a member of an apostolic — sorry I didn’t say it correctly.
That’s okay. People say apostolic and that’s perfectly fine.
Apostolic Christian church and was there a part of their doctrine that addressed popular music? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Absolutely. Absolutely. When I mentioned a second ago that I won this award for best documentary film it was actually a film about my mother’s Gospel group, the Apostolic Singers as we call it, of Miami. And that’s kind of a branch of the Pentecostal teaching in Christianity, okay, the apostolic faith is sort of under this Pentecostal thing. And while we — you know my family, everyone in my family sings, plays an instrument, something. And my grandfather played violin and guitar. He was the one that started the Apostolic Singers. He and his brother built the little community that was part of where I grew up, Perrine, Florida, Richmond Heights, Florida. That’s all kind of South of Coral Gables and Coconut Grove. So this area, I mean I was born in the mid-50s so this area was predominantly black, although we were very much a cosmopolitan and international city at the time, you know Miami Beach — some of my first gigs were on Miami Beach. This particular branch of Pentecostal faith frowns upon any connection whatsoever to making money as a musician, to actually earning money as a musician. It is, it’s sort of a, there’s a bit of a conflict, a bit of a — what is that word when you’re kind of — contradictory — where if you have a gift, and you received this gift from God and you don’t use it, you’ll lose it. There’s that one teaching. But we mean for you to use it like this. You can use it but use it like this. So we’re not encouraged to take money, you know we can get in the car and drive hundreds of miles and sing our hearts out and play and get everybody saved and make revivals and things, and you know maybe they’ll take up an offering to make sure you have gas money to get home. But that’s not the same thing as paying you for your offering, you know your service through the music. This was a very, very — this still is very much a part of the teaching and has been a conflict for most of my life. And unfortunately to this day I still have to confront that personally in my personal family life and it’s a very, very sad truth. So the answer to your question is yes, there are — I have an aunt who is in this film, it’s called “Northing But the Blood.” And she was my first real piano teacher without being my piano teacher because — physically — because she was the accompanist for the Apostolic Singers when I was about four or five years old and she still does it. And she’s in the film. And she’s still accompanying. You know she was at church Sunday somewhere playing for someone. Okay? And she’s 82 now. And she still has issues with that. She still confronts, at this time in her life with all of that skill, being able to simply receive payment for her work. I’ve encouraged her in the last maybe twenty years to just allow herself, and give herself permission to just be rewarded however people choose to.
